Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 49, verse 1:

Tafsir of Surat al-Hujurat. It is Medinan by consensus (ijma'). It has eighteen verses. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O you who believe, do not put yourselves forward before Allah and His Messenger, and fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾ (1)

In it there are three issues.

The first: the words of the Exalted, ﴿O you who believe, do not put yourselves forward before Allah and His Messenger﴾. The scholars said: among the Arabs there was harshness and bad manners in addressing the Prophet (ﷺ) and in giving nicknames to people. So the surah is concerned with commanding noble character and observing proper conduct (adab). Al-Dahhak and Ya'qub al-Hadrami read "la taqaddamu" with a fatha on the ta' and the dal, from taqaddum (advancing). The rest read "tuqaddimu" with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the dal, from taqdim (putting forward). Their meanings are clear: do not put forward, in word or deed, anything before the word and deed of Allah and of His Messenger, in matters that you should take from him, whether of religion or of worldly affairs. Whoever puts his own word or deed ahead of the Messenger (ﷺ) has put it ahead of Allah the Exalted, because the Messenger (ﷺ) only commands by the command of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

The second: There is disagreement about the occasion of its revelation, in six opinions.

The first: what al-Wahidi mentioned from the hadith of Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibn Abi Mulaykah told me that Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr informed him that a caravan of Banu Tamim came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Abu Bakr said: "Appoint al-Qa'qa' ibn Ma'bad." Umar said: "Appoint al-Aqra' ibn Habis." Abu Bakr said: "You only intended to oppose me." Umar said: "I did not intend to oppose you." They kept arguing until their voices rose, and in that regard this was revealed: "O you who believe, do not put yourselves forward before Allah and His Messenger – up to His words – and if they had patiently waited until you came out to them." Al-Bukhari narrated it from al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn al-Sabbah; al-Mahdawi also mentioned it.

The second: it is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) wished to appoint a man as deputy over Medina when he went to Khaybar, and Umar advised him to appoint another man, so this was revealed: "O you who believe, do not put yourselves forward before Allah and His Messenger." Al-Mahdawi also mentioned it.

The third: what al-Mawardi mentioned from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: The Prophet (ﷺ) sent twenty-four men from his companions to Banu Amir, and they killed them, except for three who lagged behind and were spared, and they returned [[ankafa al-qawm inkifa': they went back and dispersed.]] to Medina. They met two men from Banu Sulaym and asked them about their lineage. They said: "From Banu Amir," because they thought Banu Amir were more honorable than Banu Sulaym, so they killed the two. A group from Banu Sulaym came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "There is a covenant between us and you, and two of our men have been killed." The Prophet (ﷺ) paid their blood money of one hundred camels, and this verse was revealed to him concerning their killing of the two men. Qatadah said: some people used to say, "If only such-and-such had been revealed about me, if only such-and-such had been revealed about me," so this verse was revealed. Ibn Abbas said: they were forbidden to speak before his speech. Mujahid said: do not presume [[iftata al-kalam: he invented it. Iftata 'alayhi fi al-amr: he ruled on it. Iftata bi-ra'yihi: he acted on his own opinion alone.]] against Allah and His Messenger until Allah decides through the tongue of His Messenger; al-Bukhari also mentioned it. Al-Hasan said: it was revealed concerning a people who slaughtered before the Prophet (ﷺ) had prayed, so he commanded them to repeat the slaughter. Ibn Jurayj said: do not put forward acts of obedience before their appointed time, which Allah the Exalted and His Messenger (ﷺ) have set.

I say: these five later opinions were mentioned by al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi, and al-Mawardi had listed them before him. Al-Qadi said: all of them are sound and fall under the general meaning, but Allah knows best what the actual cause that prompted the verse was, and perhaps it was revealed without a specific cause, and Allah knows best. Al-Qadi said: if we say it was revealed concerning putting acts of worship ahead of their times, that is correct, because every act of worship that is fixed to a time may not be performed before it, such as prayer, fasting and pilgrimage, and that is clear. Except that the scholars differed concerning zakat, since it is a financial act of worship and is required for a known purpose, namely meeting the need of the poor; and because the Prophet (ﷺ) asked al-Abbas for two years' zakat in advance; and because of what has come concerning gathering the zakat al-fitr before the day of Eid al-Fitr, so that it may be given to its deserving recipients on the day it becomes obligatory, which is the day of Eid al-Fitr. All of this implies that it is permissible to advance it by a year or two. If the new year arrives and the nisab is in the same state, it falls into its proper place. If the new year arrives and the nisab has changed, it becomes clear that it was a voluntary charity. Ashhab said: it is not permissible to advance it even for a moment before the year is complete, just as with prayer; he seems to have applied the principle of acts of worship, seeing it as one of the pillars of Islam, and so he gave it its due in order and good arrangement. The rest of our scholars held that advancing a small amount of it is permissible, because it is pardoned in the law, unlike a large amount. What Ashhab said is more sound, for distinguishing the small from the large is valid in the principles of the Shariah, but this is for reasons that apply specifically to the small and not the large. As for our issue, the day in this respect is like the month, and the month like the year. So it is either a complete advance, as Abu Hanifah and al-Shafi'i said, or else preserving the act of worship at its appointed time, as Ashhab said.

The third: the words of the Exalted, ﴿do not put yourselves forward before Allah﴾, are a principle for refraining from confronting the sayings of the Prophet (ﷺ), and for making it obligatory to follow him and emulate him. Likewise the Prophet (ﷺ) said during his illness: "Tell Abu Bakr to lead the people in prayer." Aisha said to Hafsah, may Allah be pleased with them both: "Tell him that Abu Bakr is a tender-hearted man [[asif: quick to weep and grieve. It was also said: he is gentle of heart.]], and that whenever he stands in your place he will not make the people hear because of his weeping, so command Umar to lead the people in prayer." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "You are indeed like the women of Joseph [[al-Qastallani said: "that is, like them in showing something contrary to what is within, for Aisha showed that her reason for wanting the leadership of prayer removed from al-Siddiq was that he would not make the followers hear the recitation because of his weeping, while her real aim was more than that, namely that people would not regard him as a bad omen. This is like Zulaykha, who summoned the women and showed honor by hospitality, while her purpose was that they would look at Joseph's beauty and excuse her for loving him; he used the plural in his words 'you' while meaning Aisha alone, and the word 'companions' while meaning Zulaykha alone."]]. Tell Abu Bakr to lead the people in prayer." So the meaning of His words, "companions of Joseph," is temptation by turning away from what is permissible to what is not permissible.

Some who hold the view of analogy (qiyas) have sometimes cited this verse as evidence. This is invalid on their part, for whatever has its proof established, there is no putting forward before him in acting upon it. The evidence of the Book and the Sunnah has established the obligation of acting by analogy in the branches of the Shariah, so there is no putting forward before him in that.

"And fear Allah": that is, in the putting forward that is forbidden. "Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing": of your speech. "All-Knowing": of your deeds.

There are six issues in this passage.

**The first issue:** the words of God Most High, ﴿O you who believe, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet﴾. Al-Bukhari and al-Tirmidhi narrated from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, who said: Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr told me that al-Aqra' ibn Habis came to the Prophet ﷺ. Abu Bakr said, "O Messenger of God, appoint him over his people." Umar said, "Do not appoint him, O Messenger of God." So the two of them argued in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ until their voices rose. Abu Bakr said to Umar, "You only intended to oppose me." Umar said, "I did not intend to oppose you." He said: then this verse was revealed: "O you who believe, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet." He said: after that, whenever Umar spoke in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ, he would not be heard until he had asked him to repeat it. He said: Ibn al-Zubayr did not mention his grandfather, meaning Abu Bakr. He said: this is a hadith that is *gharib* (rare, with a single or unusual transmission) and *hasan* (good). Some of them narrated it from Ibn Abi Mulaykah as a *mursal* (a report in which the companion is omitted from the chain), without mentioning Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr. I say: that is al-Bukhari. He said, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah: "The two good men, Abu Bakr and Umar, nearly perished. They raised their voices in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ when the caravan of Banu Tamim arrived to him. One of them pointed to al-Aqra' ibn Habis, brother of Banu Mujashi', and the other pointed to another man." Nafi' said: I do not remember his name. Abu Bakr said to Umar, "You only intended to oppose me." He said, "I did not intend to oppose you." Their voices rose over this, so God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: "O you who believe, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet," the verse. Ibn al-Zubayr said: after this verse, Umar did not make the Messenger of God ﷺ hear him until he had asked him to repeat it.

Al-Mahdawi reported from Ali, may God be pleased with him: the words "do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet" were revealed about us, when our voices rose, myself, Ja'far and Zayd ibn Harithah, as we disputed over the daughter of Hamzah when Zayd brought her from Makkah. The Messenger of God ﷺ ruled in favour of Ja'far, because her maternal aunt was with him. This hadith has already been mentioned in *Al 'Imran* (see vol. 4, p. 88).

In the two *Sahihs* (al-Bukhari and Muslim) it is narrated from Anas ibn Malik that the Prophet ﷺ missed Thabit ibn Qays. A man said, "O Messenger of God, I will find out for you what has happened to him." He went to him and found him sitting in his house with his head bowed. He said to him, "What is your condition?" He replied, "Evil! He used to raise his voice above the voice of the Prophet ﷺ, so his deeds have been nullified and he is among the people of the Fire." (The shift from the speaker to the third person here is a *iltifat*, and the original would be: "I used to raise my voice.") The man came to the Prophet ﷺ and informed him that he had said such and such. Musa (this is Ibn Anas, one of the narrators in the chain) said: so he returned to him the second time with a great glad tidings, and he said: "Go to him and tell him that you are not among the people of the Fire, but you are among the people of Paradise." This is the wording of al-Bukhari.

This Thabit is Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas al-Khazraji, whose kunyah (teknonym) was Abu Muhammad, after his son Muhammad. It was also said: Abu Abd al-Rahman. He was killed on the day of al-Harrah, leaving three sons: Muhammad, Yahya and Abdullah. He was an eloquent orator, well known for that; he was called "the orator of the Messenger of God ﷺ," just as Hassan was called "the poet of the Messenger of God ﷺ." [Al-Harrah: a land on the outskirts of Madinah with large black stones, known as Harrat Waqim. In it took place the battle in the year sixty-three after the Hijrah, in the days of Yazid ibn Mu'awiyah, when his army from the people of Syria, whom he had dispatched to fight the people of Madinah, including companions and Successors, plundered the city; he appointed Muslim ibn Uqbah al-Murri over them.]

When the delegation of Tamim came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and asked for a contest in boasting, their orator stood and boasted. Then Thabit ibn Qays stood and gave an eloquent, forceful speech and overcame them. Their poet, who was al-Aqra' ibn Habis, stood and recited:

We came to you so that people would know our merit,
and if they dispute with us when the noble deeds are mentioned...

And we are the heads of the people from every group,
and there is none in the land of the Hijaz like Darim.

And for us is the *mirba'* (the chief's share, a quarter of the spoils) in every raid
that takes place in Najd or in the lowlands of Tihama. [In the biography of Ibn Hisham: "...or in the land of the non-Arabs." The *mirba'* is what the chief takes, a quarter of the booty.]

Then Hassan stood and said:

O Banu Darim, do not boast, for your boasting
will return as a burden when noble deeds are mentioned.

You are lost! You boast over us, while you
are our servants, a mix of wet-nurses and servants. [Hablitum: you have lost. Al-khawal: a man's retinue and followers.]

These were verses of theirs, in a number of lines. They said: "Their orator is more eloquent than our orator, and their poet is a better poet than our poet." Their voices rose, so God Most High revealed: "Do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet, nor speak loudly to him in speech."

Ata al-Khurasani said: the daughter of Thabit ibn Qays told me: when the verse "O you who believe, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet" was revealed, her father entered his house, closed his door behind him, and the Prophet ﷺ missed him. He sent for him to ask about his state. He said, "I am a man with a loud voice; I fear that my deeds have been nullified." He ﷺ said: "You are not one of them; rather you will live in goodness and die in goodness." She said: then God revealed: "Indeed God does not love everyone who is self-conceited and boastful" (Qur'an 31:18). Then he closed his door and began to weep. The Prophet ﷺ missed him, sent for him, and was informed. He said, "O Messenger of God, I love beauty, and I love that my people should make me their chief." He ﷺ said: "You are not one of them; rather you will live praised, be killed as a martyr, and enter Paradise." She said: when the day of Yamamah came, he went out with Khalid ibn al-Walid against Musaylimah. When they met, the Muslims were routed. Thabit and Salim, the client of Abu Hudhayfah, said: "This is not how we fought with the Messenger of God ﷺ." Then each of them dug a pit for himself, stood firm, fought, and both were killed. On Thabit that day was a precious coat of mail. A man from the Muslims passed by him and took it. Then, while a Muslim man was sleeping, Thabit came to him in a dream and said: "I charge you with a bequest, and beware of saying, 'This is a dream,' and neglecting it. When I was killed yesterday, a man from the Muslims passed by me and took my coat of mail. His dwelling is at the farthest edge of the people, and beside his tent is a horse pulling at its tether. He has put a cooking pot over the coat of mail, and above the pot is a saddle. Go to Khalid and order him to send for my coat of mail so that he takes it. When you come to Madinah, go to the Khalifah of the Messenger of God ﷺ, that is Abu Bakr, and say to him: 'I owe such and such a debt, and such and such of my slaves are freed,' and so on." The man went to Khalid and informed him. Khalid sent for the coat of mail, it was brought, and he told Abu Bakr about his vision, and Abu Bakr approved his bequest.

He said: we know of no one whose bequest was approved after his death except Thabit, may God have mercy on him. Abu Umar mentioned this in *al-Isti'ab*.

**The second issue:** the words of God Most High, ﴿and do not speak loudly to him in speech﴾. That is, do not address him as "O Muhammad" or "O Ahmad," but say "O Prophet of God" or "O Messenger of God," out of reverence for him. It was also said: the hypocrites would raise their voices in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ so that the weaker Muslims would follow them, so the Muslims were forbidden from that. It was also said: "do not speak loudly to him" means do not speak loudly *against* him, as one says "he fell on his mouth" (*li-fihi*), meaning onto his mouth. ﴿Like the loudness of some of you to others﴾: the *kaf* here is the *kaf* of comparison in a position of accusative, meaning: do not speak loudly to him with a loudness like the loudness of some of you to others.

In this there is evidence that they were not forbidden from raising their voices absolutely, so that they could speak to him only in a whisper or in a low voice. Rather, they were forbidden from a particular kind of loudness, qualified by a description: namely, the loudness characterised by resembling what they had become accustomed to among themselves, which lacks regard for the dignity of prophethood and the greatness of its rank, and the lowering of all other ranks even if they are exalted in their own station. ﴿Lest your deeds be nullified while you do not perceive﴾: that is, so that they are not nullified, meaning annulled. This is the view of the Basrans. The Kufans said: that is, lest your deeds be nullified.

**The third issue:** the meaning of the verse is a command to glorify the Messenger of God ﷺ and to honour him, and to lower the voice in his presence and when addressing him. That is: when he speaks and you speak, you must not let your voices exceed the level at which he speaks, and you must lower them so that his speech is dominant over yours and his loudness overpowers yours, so that his superiority over you is manifest and his precedence clear, and his distinction from the mass of you is like the marking of the piebald (*al-ablaq*, a horse with white and black patches) that stands out. Do not drown out his voice with your noise, nor overwhelm his speech with your clamour.

In the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud it is: "Do not raise with your voices." Some scholars disliked raising the voice at his grave, upon him be peace. Some scholars disliked raising the voice in the gatherings of scholars, to honour them, since they are the heirs of the prophets.

**The fourth issue:** Al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi said: the sanctity of the Prophet ﷺ after death is like his sanctity in life, and his words transmitted after his death have the same standing as his words heard from his own lips. So when his speech is recited, every present person must not raise his voice above it, nor turn away from it, just as this was required of him in his assembly when he uttered it. God, glorified be He, indicated the continuing sanctity mentioned above across the passing of ages by His words: "When the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent" (Qur'an 7:204). His words ﷺ are from revelation, and they have the same wisdom as the Qur'an, except for certain exceptions whose explanation is in the books of jurisprudence.

**The fifth issue:** The purpose of raising the voice and of loudness in this verse is not what is intended for contempt and disdain, because that is disbelief, and those addressed are believers. Rather, the purpose is a sound which, in itself, and by what is heard from its tone, is unsuited to what great people are revered by and what the elders are honoured by; so one must make an effort to lower it and bring it to a level in which the commanded reverence and honour become evident. The prohibition does not also cover raising the voice in a way that would harm the Messenger of God ﷺ, such as what they did in war, or in disputing with an obstinate opponent, or in terrifying an enemy, or the like. In a hadith, he ﷺ said to al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib when the people were routed on the day of Hunayn: "Shout to the people!" Al-Abbas was the loudest of people in voice. It is reported that once a raid came upon them, and al-Abbas shouted, "Ya sabahah!" (a cry of alarm), and pregnant women miscarried because of the intensity of his voice. Concerning this, the poet of Banu Ja'dah says:

The driving away of the beasts of prey by Abu Urwah (a kunyah of al-Abbas)
when he feared they would mingle with the sheep.

The narrators claim that he used to drive wild beasts away from the sheep, and the gall of the beast would burst in its belly.

**The sixth issue:** Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿lest your deeds be nullified﴾: the estimated reading is "li-an tahbata" (so that they are nullified), meaning "fa-tahbatu a'malukum" (so your deeds are nullified). Thus the *lam* that is implied is the *lam al-sayrurah* (the lam of consequence, expressing result rather than intention). The words "lest your deeds be nullified while you do not perceive" do not necessitate that a person becomes a disbeliever while not knowing it. Just as a disbeliever does not become a believer except by his own choice of faith over disbelief, so too a believer does not become a disbeliever through something he does not intend or choose, by consensus. Likewise, a disbeliever does not become a disbeliever through something he does not know.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 49, verse 3:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who lower their voices in the presence of the Messenger of Allah﴾, that is, they lower their voices in his presence when they speak, out of reverence for him, or when they speak to someone else in his presence, out of reverence for him. Abu Hurayrah said: When "Do not raise your voices" was revealed...

Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "By Allah, I will not raise my voice except as one who confides in a close friend (akhi al-sirar)" [al-sirar (with a kasra): secret conversation, i.e., like one who speaks in secret, or like the manner of a whispered conversation, lowering his voice; the kaf is an adjectival clause modifying a deleted verbal noun].

Sunayd related: Abbad ibn al-Awwam narrated to us from Muhammad ibn Amr, from Abu Salamah, who said: When ﴿Do not put yourselves forward before Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Hujurat: 1] was revealed, Abu Bakr said: "By the One who sent you with the truth, I will not speak to you after this except as one who confides in a close friend."

Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr said: When "Do not raise your voices" was revealed, Umar did not speak in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ after that until he was asked to repeat his words, because of how low he lowered his voice. Then this was revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who lower their voices in the presence of the Messenger of Allah—those are the ones whose hearts Allah has tested for piety﴾.

Al-Farra' said: that is, He purified them for piety. Al-Akhfash said: that is, He singled them out for piety. Ibn Abbas said: "Allah tested their hearts for piety" means He purified them from every blameworthy trait and placed in their hearts the fear of Allah and piety. Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: He removed desires from their hearts.

Al-imtihan (testing) is an iftiʿal form derived from mahantu al-adim mahnan, meaning I stretched the hide until I widened it. So the meaning of "Allah tested their hearts for piety" is that He widened them and expanded them for piety. According to the preceding opinions: He tested their hearts and purified them, like your saying: "I tested the silver," meaning I examined it until it became pure. So there is an ellipsis in the speech indicated by the context, which is "purification."

Abu Amr said: Everything you exert yourself in, you have "mahantahu" (tested it). He recited:

"The she-camels came, their exhaustion visible, emaciated from travel, their flanks trembling."

[al-Radhaya: plural of radhiyyah, a camel made lean by travel. al-Kalal: exhaustion. al-Atal: plural of itl, the flank.]

﴿For them is forgiveness and a great reward﴾.

Mujahid and others said: It was revealed concerning the Bedouins of Banu Tamim. A delegation of them came to the Prophet ﷺ, entered the mosque, and called out to the Prophet ﷺ from behind his chamber: "Come out to us, for our praise is an adornment and our blame is a disgrace." They were seventy men, and they had brought the captives of their offspring as ransom. The Prophet ﷺ had been sleeping at the midday rest (al-qa'ilah).

It is also narrated that the one who called out was al-Aqra' ibn Habis, and that it was he who said: "Indeed my praise is an adornment and indeed my blame is a disgrace." The Prophet ﷺ said: "That is Allah." [Al-Tirmidhi mentioned it from al-Bara' ibn Azib as well.]

Zayd ibn Arqam narrated, saying: Some people came to the Prophet ﷺ, and some of them said to others: "Come, let us go to this man. If he is a prophet, we are the happiest of people in following him; and if he is a king, we will live in his protection" (in the Tabari text: "in his wing"). So they came to the Prophet ﷺ and began calling out to him while he was in his chamber: "O Muhammad, O Muhammad!" Then Allah the Exalted revealed this verse.

It was said: They were from Banu Tamim. Muqatil said: They were nineteen, namely: Qays ibn Asim, al-Zibriqan ibn Badr, al-Aqra' ibn Habis, Suwayd ibn Hashim, Khalid ibn Malik, Ata' ibn Habis, al-Qa'qa' ibn Ma'bad, Waki' ibn Waki', and Uyaynah ibn Hisn, who was "the foolish one who is obeyed." He was one of the great leaders, who would be followed by ten thousand spears, that is, by those who follow him. His name was Hudhayfah, and he was called Uyaynah because of a shtar (a turning inward of the eyelid) that was in his eyes. Abd al-Razzaq mentioned about this Uyaynah that he is the one concerning whom was revealed: ﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance﴾ [al-Kahf: 28]. What is sufficient was already discussed at the end of "al-A'raf" in the words spoken to Umar, may Allah be pleased with him; al-Bukhari mentioned it.

It is also narrated that they came at the time of midday while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sleeping, and they began calling out to him: "O Muhammad, O Muhammad, come out to us!" He awoke and came out, and the verse was revealed. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked, and he said: "They are the rude ones of Banu Tamim. Had they not been among the people most fiercely fighting against the one-eyed Dajjal, I would have prayed to Allah against them that He destroy them."

Al-hujurat is the plural of al-hujrah, like al-ghurufat, the plural of ghurfah, and al-zulumat, the plural of zulmah. It was said: al-hujurat is the plural of al-hujar, and al-hujar is the plural of hujrah, so it is a plural of a plural. In it there are two dialectal forms: with a damma on the jim and with a fatha on it (there is a third form: with sukun on the jim). The poet said:

When they saw us with our knees exposed, on a place where we do not mix seriousness with jesting...

Al-hujrah is a piece of land enclosed by a wall that surrounds it, and the pen for camels is called al-hujrah, and it is a form (fu'lah) in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ulah). Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' read "al-hujarat" with a fatha on the jim, to avoid the heaviness of the two dammas; and it was read "al-hujrat" with sukun on the jim, for lightness. The root meaning of the word is prevention: whatever you prevent from reaching something, you have placed a restriction (hajara) upon it. Then it is possible that the one calling out is a part of the group, and for this reason He said: "Most of them do not understand," meaning that those who call out to you are from a people in which ignorance is predominant.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 49, verse 5:

﴿And if they had been patient until you came out to them, it would have been better for them. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

That is: if they had waited for your emergence, it would have been more suitable for them in their religion and their worldly affairs. The Prophet (ﷺ) did not seclude himself from the people except at times when he was occupied with matters of his own concerns, so their disturbing him in that state was a breach of good manners. It was also said: they had come as intercessors concerning the captives of Banu Anbar, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) freed half of them and ransomed the other half. Had they been patient, he would have freed all of them without ransom. "And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful."

There are seven issues in this verse.

The first issue concerns the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿O you who believe, if a deviator brings you a report, verify it﴾. It is said that this verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt. The reason for this is what Sa'id reported on the authority of Qatadah: that the Prophet (ﷺ) sent al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah as a collector of zakat to the Banu al-Mustaliq. When they saw him, they came toward him, and he was afraid of them. In another narration: because of an enmity that existed between him and them. He returned to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him that they had apostatized from Islam. So the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) sent Khalid ibn al-Walid and instructed him to verify the matter and not to hasten. Khalid set out and came to them at night, and he sent his scouts. When they came back, they informed Khalid that the people were holding firmly to Islam, and they had heard their call to prayer and their prayers. When morning came, Khalid went to them and saw that what they had described was true. He then returned to the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him, and this verse was revealed. The Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) would say: "Deliberation is from Allah, and haste is from Satan." In another narration: the Prophet (ﷺ) sent him to the Banu al-Mustaliq after they had embraced Islam. When they heard of him, they rode out to meet him. When he heard of them, he feared them and returned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him that the people had intended to kill him and had withheld their zakat. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) resolved to fight them. While they were in this state, their delegation arrived before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, we heard of your messenger and went out to him to honor him and to hand over to him the zakat that was with us. Then he turned back. We have been informed that he claims to the Messenger of Allah that we went out to fight him. By Allah, we did not go out for that." So Allah, the Exalted, revealed this verse. Al-Walid was called a "fasiq," meaning a liar. Ibn Zayd, Muqatil and Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah said: the fasiq is the liar. Abu al-Hasan [in some copies: "Abu al-Husayn"] al-Warraq said: he is one who openly commits sin. Ibn Tahir said: he is one who has no shame before Allah. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿fatathabbatu﴾ (verify), from tathabbut (verification). The rest read ﴿fatabayyanu﴾ (investigate), from tabyin (clarification). ﴿Lest you harm a people﴾ means: lest you harm them. Here "an" (lest) is in a position of nasb (accusative) by the removal of the preposition. ﴿In ignorance﴾ means: in error. ﴿And then become regretful for what you have done﴾ means: regretful over the haste and the abandonment of deliberation.

The second issue: this verse is evidence for the acceptance of the report of a single narrator (khabar al-wahid) when he is 'adl (upright and trustworthy), because it only commands verification when reporting the news of a fasiq. Whoever's deviance is established, his statement regarding reports is invalidated by consensus (ijma'), because a report is a trust and deviance is an indicator that nullifies it. The consensus has excepted from this general rule matters relating to claims and denials, and the establishment of a right due from another. For example, if someone says, "This is my slave," his statement is accepted. If he says, "So-and-so has sent this to you as a gift," that is accepted. Likewise, the report of a disbeliever is accepted in such matters. Similarly, if a person acknowledges a right owed to another against himself, it is not invalidated, by consensus. As for making a contract on behalf of another, al-Shafi'i and others said: he may not act as a guardian (wali) in marriage. Abu Hanifah and Malik said: he may act as guardian, because he manages her property, so he manages her marriage, just like a trustworthy person. Although he is deviant in his religion, his jealousy is complete, and by it he protects the sanctity of the household, and he may spend money and preserve honor. And when he is entrusted with wealth, marriage is more fitting for him.

The third issue: Ibn al-'Arabi said: It is strange that al-Shafi'i and his peers permit a deviant to lead prayer. How can one who cannot be trusted with a grain of wealth be trusted with a qintar (a large sum) of religion? The origin of this was that the rulers who led the people in prayer had corrupt religions, and it was not possible to abandon prayer behind them, nor was it possible to remove them, so people prayed with them and behind them. As 'Uthman said: "Prayer is the best of what people do. If they do well, then do well with them, and if they do evil, then avoid their evil." Then among the people were those who, when they prayed with them out of taqiyyah (precaution), would repeat the prayer for Allah's sake, and among them were those who made it their prayer. I hold that repetition is obligatory. Thus no one should abandon prayer with imams he does not approve of, but he should repeat it secretly within himself and not make this known to others.

The fourth issue: as for his rulings, if he is a ruler, he executes those that agree with the truth and rejects those that oppose it, and his ruling that he has enacted is in no way annulled. Do not pay attention to any statement other than this, whether a narration that is transmitted [in Ibn al-'Arabi: "that is related"] or an opinion that is reported, for the discussion is extensive and the truth is clear.

The fifth issue: There is no disagreement that it is valid for a person to be a messenger on behalf of another in conveying a statement, delivering an item, or informing of permission, provided that it does not go beyond the rights of the sender and the recipient. If the right of someone other than these two is involved, his statement is not accepted. This is permitted because of the necessity that calls for it, for if no one but the upright were to handle these matters among people, nothing would be achieved, due to their absence in this respect. And Allah knows best.

The sixth issue: The verse is also evidence against the view of those who say that all Muslims are upright until a disparagement (jarh) is established. This is because Allah, the Exalted, commanded verification before acceptance, and verification has no meaning after the ruling has been executed. If a judge rules before verification, he has harmed the one against whom he ruled through ignorance.

The seventh issue: If he judges by what is most likely to be true (ghalib al-zann), that is not acting in ignorance, such as judging by two upright witnesses, or accepting the statement of a qualified scholar (mujtahid). Acting in ignorance is only accepting the statement of one by whom a dominant assumption of truth is not attained. Al-Qushayri mentioned this issue, and al-Mahdawi mentioned the one before it.

And know that among you is the Messenger of Allah ﴿وَاعْلَمُوا أَنَّ فِيكُمْ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ﴾ , so do not lie, for Allah will inform him of your reports and you will be exposed.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 49, verse 9 (part 1 of 2):

There are ten issues concerning this verse.

The first issue concerns the words of God Most High: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight, then make peace between them﴾. Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman narrated from Anas ibn Malik, who said: I said, "O Prophet of God, what if you went to 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy?" So the Prophet (ﷺ) set out to him, riding a donkey, and the Muslims set out walking. The land was saline (sabakhah). When the Prophet (ﷺ) reached him, he said: "Keep away from me! By God, the stench of your donkey has harmed me." A man from the Ansar said: "By God, the donkey of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) is better smelling than you." Then a man from Ibn Ubayy's people became angry for him, and each of the two men's companions became angry for his man. So there was fighting between them with palm stalks, hands and sandals. We were told that this verse was revealed concerning them.

Mujahid said: It was revealed concerning the Aws and the Khazraj. Mujahid said: Two clans of the Ansar fought with staves and sandals, and then the verse was revealed. Similarly, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: between the Aws and the Khazraj, during the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), there was fighting with palm fronds, sandals and the like, so God revealed this verse concerning them.

Qatadah said: It was revealed concerning two men from the Ansar between whom there was a dispute (mudara'ah) over a right they shared,[[Tadara'a al-qawm: they pushed one another in the dispute or the like, and disagreed.]] so one of them said: "I will take my right by force, because of the large number of my kinsmen." The other invited him to bring their case before the Messenger of God (ﷺ), but he refused to follow him. The matter continued between them until they clashed, and some of them struck others with hands, sandals and swords, and then this verse was revealed.

Al-Kalbi said: It was revealed concerning the war between Sumayr and Hatib,[[See the account of their war in al-Kamil of Ibn al-Athir, vol. 1, p. 494, printed in Europe.]] and Sumayr had killed Hatib. So the Aws and the Khazraj fought until the Prophet (ﷺ) came to them, and then it was revealed. God commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers to make peace between them.

Al-Suddi said: There was a woman from the Ansar called "Umm Zayd," who was married to a man who was not from the Ansar. She quarrelled with her husband; she wanted to visit her people, but her husband detained her and put her in an upper room (illiyyah) that none of her family could enter. The woman sent word to her people, and her people came and brought her down so they could take her away. The man went out and called for help from his family, and his cousins came out to prevent the woman from reaching her family. They pushed against one another and struck each other with sandals, and then the verse was revealed.

The word "ta'ifah" (group) applies to a single man, to a plural, and to two, so this is an instance of the meaning being taken into account rather than the wording, because "the two groups" carries the sense of "people" and "folk."

In the reading of 'Abd Allah it is: "until they return to the command of God; and if they return, then make peace between them with justice." Ibn Abi Ablah read "iqtatalata" (the dual feminine verb), following the wording of "the two groups." The discussion of this was already given at the end of Surah Bara'ah.[[See vol. 8, p. 5 (294).]]

Ibn 'Abbas, commenting on the words of God, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿And let a group of the believers witness their punishment﴾ [al-Nur 24:2], said: "One man or more, and a ta'ifah of a thing is a piece of it."

"Then make peace between them": by calling them to the Book of God, whether for them or against them. "And if one of them transgresses against the other": it oversteps and does not respond to the judgment of God and His Book. Baghy (transgression, rebellion) means overbearing and corruption. "Then fight the one that transgresses until it returns to the command of God," that is, returns to His Book. "And if it returns," that is, comes back, "then make peace between them with justice," that is, compel them to fairness. "And act justly," O people, "so that you do not fight." It has been said: aqsitu means "be just." "Indeed God loves the just," that is, those who are fair and upright.

The second issue: The scholars said: The two parties of the Muslims in their fighting are not free of one of two situations: either both of them fight in a manner of transgression on both sides, or not. If it is the first, then what is obligatory is that one should intervene between them with whatever reconciles them and brings about restraint and truce. If they do not separate and do not make peace, and they persist in transgression, then one must turn to fighting them both. As for the second situation, which is that one of them is transgressing against the other, then what is obligatory is to fight the transgressing party until it desists and repents. If it does so, then reconciliation is to be made between it and the party it transgressed against, with equity and justice. If the fighting between them breaks out because of a doubt (shubhah) that has entered them, and both of them consider themselves to be in the right, then what is obligatory is to remove the doubt by clear proof and decisive arguments pointing to the paths of truth. If they ride the stubbornness (lajaj) and do not act in accordance with what they were guided to and advised of, namely following the truth after it has become clear to them, then they have joined the transgressing parties. And God knows best.

The third issue: This verse is evidence for the obligation to fight a transgressing party whose transgression is known, whether against the imam or against any of the Muslims. It also refutes the view of one who forbids fighting against believers, and who argues from his words, peace be upon him: "Fighting a believer is disbelief." If fighting a transgressing believer were disbelief, God would have commanded disbelief, exalted is God above that! Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, fought those who held to Islam but refused to pay zakat; he ordered that no one who fled should be pursued, that no wounded man should be finished off, and their property was not made lawful (for seizure), unlike the situation with disbelievers.

Al-Tabari said: If the obligation in every dispute that arises between the two sides were to flee from it and remain in one's dwelling, then no legal punishment (hadd) would ever be enforced and no falsehood would ever be nullified. The people of hypocrisy and immorality would find a way to make lawful everything God has forbidden them, such as the property of the Muslims, the taking of their women captive, and the shedding of their blood, by forming factions against them while the Muslims withheld their hands from them. This would contradict his words, peace be upon him: "Take hold of the hands of your foolish ones."

The fourth issue: Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: This verse is the foundation for fighting among Muslims and the principal reference in the war against those who interpret (al-muta'awwilin). The Companions relied upon it, and the notable figures of the community resorted to it. It was the verse the Prophet (ﷺ) had in mind when he said: "The rebellious party will kill 'Ammar."[[This is 'Ammar ibn Yasir; see his account in the books on the Companions.]] His words, peace be upon him, concerning the Khawarij (Kharijites) were: "They will come out at the best of the groups, or at a time of division." The first narration is the more sound, because of his words, peace be upon him: "The party nearest to the truth will kill them." It was 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and those with him who killed them.

It has thus been established among the scholars of the Muslims, and proven by the evidence of the religion, that 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, was the imam, and that anyone who rebels against him is a transgressor, and that fighting him is obligatory until he returns to the truth and submits to reconciliation. This is because 'Uthman, may God be pleased with him, was killed while the Companions were innocent of his blood, since he forbade fighting against those who rose against him, saying: "I will not be the first to succeed the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in his community by killing." So he endured the trial, submitted to the ordeal, and sacrificed himself for the community.

Then it was not possible to leave the people unguided (sudan), so the matter was presented to the remaining Companions whom 'Umar mentioned in the consultation (shura),[[Added from Ibn al-'Arabi.]] and they deferred it to one another. 'Ali, may God honour his face, was the most entitled to it and most fit for it, so he accepted it as a precaution (hawtah) for the community, so that its blood would not be shed through mutual attacks and falsehood, or so that its affairs would not be torn apart into something that could not be contained. Perhaps the religion would have changed and the pillar of Islam would have collapsed.

When he was given the pledge of allegiance, the people of Syria demanded, as a condition of the pledge, that they be enabled to seize the murderers of 'Uthman and exact retaliation (qawad) from them. 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, said to them: "Enter into the pledge, and seek the right, and you will attain it." They said: "A pledge is not valid while the murderers of 'Uthman are with you; you see them morning and evening." 'Ali was firmer in his view on this and more correct in his statement, because if he had undertaken retaliation against them, tribes would have rallied to their side, and it would have become a third war. So he waited for them until the matter was secured (yastawthiq al-amr)[[In Ibn al-'Arabi: "al-amn" (security).]] and the pledge was concluded, and the demand was made by the heirs in a session of judgment, so that judgment would proceed in accordance with the truth.

There is no disagreement among the community that it is permissible for the imam to delay retaliation (qisas) when doing so would lead to inciting strife (fitnah) or scattering the unity of the community.

Likewise, this is what happened with Talhah and al-Zubayr. They neither deposed 'Ali from his authority nor objected to him concerning his religious integrity; they only considered that beginning with the killing of 'Uthman's companions was preferable.

I say: This is an account of the cause of the war that took place between them. Some of the eminent scholars said: The battle at Basra between them was not by deliberate intention to fight, but suddenly, by way of each of the two sides defending itself, because each believed that the other side had betrayed it. For the matter had been settled between them, and the truce and dispersal had been completed by mutual consent. But the murderers of 'Uthman, may God be pleased with him, feared being handed over to them and surrounded by them, so they gathered, consulted and disagreed. Then their opinions agreed upon dividing into two groups and beginning the fighting at dawn in both armies, and that the arrows should fly between them, and that the group in 'Ali's army should cry out: "Talhah and al-Zubayr have betrayed!" and the group in the army of Talhah and al-Zubayr should cry: "'Ali has betrayed!" So this came to pass as they had planned, and the war broke out. Each side was defending its own position in its own mind and preventing its own blood from being wasted (al-ishatah).[[Al-ishatah: destruction. It is said: "Ashata fulan dam fulan" when he exposed him to destruction.]] This was correct on both sides and obedience to God Most High, since the fighting and the refraining from it came about in this manner. This is the sound and well-known view. And God knows best.

The fifth issue: The words of God Most High, ﴿then fight the one that transgresses until it returns to the command of God﴾, are a command to fight. It is an obligation of sufficiency (fard kifayah): when some of the community undertake it, it is lifted from the rest. For this reason, some Companions, may God be pleased with them, held back from these positions, such as Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, Muhammad ibn Maslamah and others. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib confirmed their decision, and each of them offered an excuse to him that he accepted.

It is narrated that when the affair came to Mu'awiyah, may God be pleased with him, he reproached Sa'd for what he had done, and said to him: "You were not among those who made peace between the two groups when they fought, nor among those who fought the transgressing group." Sa'd said to him: "I regret my abstention from fighting the transgressing group." Thus it becomes clear that there is no liability (darak)[[Al-darak (with the letter ra' vowelled or unvowelled): consequence, liability.]] on everyone for what he did; rather it was an action based on personal judgment (ijtihad) and an application of the requirement of the Law. And God knows best.

The sixth issue: The words of God Most High, ﴿And if it returns, then make peace between them with justice﴾. Part of justice in their reconciliation is that they should not be held to account for the blood or property that passed between them, since that was a loss incurred under interpretation (ta'wil). Demanding it would drive them away from reconciliation and would cause the transgression to grow more stubborn.[[Istasha al-rajul fi al-amr: he became obstinate. And the affairs: they grew severe and great.]] This is a principle regarding the public interest (maslahah). The spokesman of the community (lisan al-ummah) has said: The wisdom of God in the war among the Companions was to make known to them the rulings concerning fighting people of interpretation, since the rulings concerning fighting the people of polytheism had already been made known through the words and practice of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

**The seventh issue:** If an unjust rebel group (*khārijah bāghiyah*) rises against a just ruler (*imam 'adl*) and has no valid justification, the ruler shall fight them with the whole Muslim community or with a sufficient portion of it. Before that, he shall call them to obedience and to re-entering the community. If they refuse to return and make peace, they shall be fought. Their captives shall not be killed, their fleeing shall not be pursued, their wounded shall not be finished off (*tadhfīf*, meaning to deliver the final blow to a wounded person and make sure he dies), and neither their offspring nor their property shall be taken as spoils. If a just person kills a rebel, or a rebel kills a just person who is his guardian (*walī*), they shall not inherit from each other. A person who kills intentionally shall never inherit from his victim under any circumstances. It has also been said that the just person inherits from the rebel, by analogy with retaliation (*qiṣāṣ*).

**The eighth issue:** Whatever blood or property the rebels and the Khawārij (the Khawarij, an early seceding sect) destroyed, and then repented, they shall not be held liable for. Abu Hanifa said: they shall be liable. Al-Shafi'i has two opinions. Abu Hanifa's reasoning is that this is destruction through transgression, so compensation is obligatory. Our reliance in this matter is that the Companions, may God be pleased with them, in their wars did not pursue fleeing men, did not finish off the wounded, did not kill captives, and did not hold anyone liable for life or property, and they are the model to follow. Ibn Umar said: the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O servant of God, do you know what God's ruling is concerning those of this community who rebel?" He said: "God and His Messenger know best." He said: "Their wounded shall not be finished off, their captives shall not be killed, their fleeing shall not be pursued, and their spoils shall not be divided." As for what still exists in its original form, it shall be returned as it is. All of this applies to those who rebelled on the basis of an interpretation (*ta'wīl*) that justifies them for themselves. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned in his tafsir: If the rebel group is so small in number that it has no strength, it is liable for what it did after returning to obedience. If it is numerous, possessing strength and power, it is not liable, except according to Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, may God have mercy on him, who used to rule that liability falls upon them when they return. As for before they have gathered and mobilized, or when they disperse once the war has laid down its burdens, what they have damaged they are liable for by the consensus (*ijmā'*) of all. Therefore, reading the reconciliation "with justice" in His words, "then make peace between them with justice," in accordance with the view of Muhammad is clear and fits the wording of the revelation. According to the view of others, it may be understood as applying to a rebel group that is small in number. What they mentioned, that the purpose is to extinguish grudges and remove resentments without liability for the offenses, is not the fine balance commanded by the practice of justice and the observance of equity. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, why did He join justice to the second reconciliation but not the first? I answer: because fighting at the beginning of the verse means that the two groups fight as rebels or as those acting on a dubious basis. Whichever of them it is, the obligation upon the Muslims in their matter is to reconcile between them, calm the masses by showing them the truth, giving effective admonitions and removing the doubt. Only when they have gone to war is fighting then obligatory. As for liability, it does not apply in that case. But if one of the two groups rebels, liability applies under both of the aforementioned views.

**The ninth issue:** If the rebels seize control of a town, collect the alms (*ṣadaqāt*), establish the prescribed punishments (*ḥudūd*), and rule its people by their judgments, the alms collected will not be taken again from the people, nor will the prescribed punishments be repeated. Their judgments shall not be overturned, except what contradicts the Book, the Sunnah, or the consensus, just as the judgments of the people of justice and Sunnah are overturned. This is the view of Mutarrif and Ibn al-Majishun. Ibn al-Qasim said: it is never permissible. It is also narrated from Asbagh that it is permissible, and also narrated from him that it is not permissible, in agreement with Ibn al-Qasim. This is also the view of Abu Hanifa, because it is an action without right by someone whose appointment is not valid, so it is not permissible, just as if they had not been rebels. Our strongest proof is what we have mentioned before, that when the turmoil subsided and the dispute ended through truce and reconciliation, the Companions, may God be pleased with them, did not challenge any of them regarding a ruling. Ibn al-'Arabi said: What I think is that this does not hold, because when the turmoil subsided, the imam himself was the rebel, and there was no one to challenge him. And God knows best.

**The tenth issue:** It is not permissible to attribute to any of the Companions a definite error, since they all exerted independent reasoning (*ijtihād*) in what they did, and they all intended God, the Mighty and Majestic. All of them are imams for us. We have been commanded to refrain from speaking about what passed between them, and not to mention them except in the best manner, out of respect for their companionship, in obedience to the Prophet's (ﷺ) prohibition against reviling them, and because God forgave them and declared His pleasure with them. In addition, there are reports from various chains of narration from the Prophet (ﷺ) that Talha is a martyr walking on the face of the earth. If what he went out for in the war had been disobedience, he would not be a martyr by being killed in it. Likewise, if what he went out for had been an error in interpretation and a shortcoming in an obligation upon him, martyrdom would still not be attained, because martyrdom is only through being killed in obedience. Therefore, their situation must be understood in the way we have explained. Among the things that prove this is what is authentically established and widely transmitted from Ali, that the killer of al-Zubayr is in the Fire, and his saying: "I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: 'Give the killer of Ibn Safiyya the good news of the Fire.'" Since this is the case, it is established that Talha and al-Zubayr were neither disobedient nor sinful by fighting, because if that had been the case, the Prophet (ﷺ) would not have said of Talha: "a martyr," and would not have informed us that the killer of al-Zubayr is in the Fire. The same applies to whoever stayed aside without error in interpretation, but rather with correct judgment as God showed him through independent reasoning. Given this, it does not require cursing them, disavowing them, declaring them wicked, nullifying their virtues and their struggle, or their great service to the religion. May God be pleased with them. Some of them were asked about the blood that was shed among them, and he said: "That is a community that has passed away; theirs is what they earned, and yours is what you have earned, and you will not be questioned about what they used to do" (Qur'an 2:134 — 2:141). Another of them was also asked about it and said: "That is blood which God has kept clean from my hands, so I will not stain my tongue with it," meaning in guarding against falling into error and judging some of them as not being right in what they did. Ibn Furak said: Some of our companions said that the way of the disputes that occurred among the Companions is like the way of what happened between the brothers of Joseph and Joseph; then they did not leave the bounds of guardianship (*wilāya*) and prophethood because of it. Likewise is the matter with what occurred among the Companions. Al-Muhasibi said: As for the blood, the matter has become unclear to us because of their disagreement. Al-Hasan al-Basri was asked about their fighting and said: "It was a fighting witnessed by the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) while we were absent; they knew while we were ignorant; they agreed and we followed; they disagreed and we paused." Al-Muhasibi said: So we say what al-Hasan said, and we know that those people knew better than us what they entered into. We follow what they agreed upon, we pause at what they disagreed upon, and we do not invent an opinion of our own. We know that they exerted independent reasoning and intended God, the Mighty and Majestic, since they were not suspected in matters of religion. And we ask God for success.

**Third-person commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 49, verse 10:**

There are three issues in this verse.

**The first issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the believers are but brothers﴾. That is, brothers in religion and in sanctity, not in lineage. For this reason it has been said: The brotherhood of religion is more enduring than the brotherhood of lineage, for the brotherhood of lineage is severed by opposition in religion, whereas the brotherhood of religion is not severed by opposition in lineage. In the two Sahihs (al-Sahihayn, the Sahih of al-Bukhari and the Sahih of Muslim), on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not envy one another, do not hate one another, do not spy on one another, do not eavesdrop (tahassus, with a ḥā'), do not engage in najash (outbidding), and be servants of Allah as brothers." (Tahassus, with a ḥā', is listening to the conversation of a people. Najash is that you increase the price of a commodity while having no desire to buy it. It has also been said that it is inciting others to buy.)

In another narration: "Do not envy one another, do not engage in najash, do not hate one another, do not turn away from one another (tadabbur), and let none of you sell over the sale of another. Be servants of Allah as brothers. The Muslim is the brother of the Muslim: he does not wrong him, does not forsake him, and does not despise him. Piety is here," and he pointed to his chest three times, "it is enough evil for a man to despise his Muslim brother. Every Muslim is sacred to the Muslim: his blood, his property, and his honour." (This is the wording of Muslim.)

In a source other than the two Sahihs, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The Muslim is the brother of the Muslim: he does not wrong him, does not blame him, does not forsake him, and does not domineer over him in building, so as to block the wind from him without his permission. He does not harm him with the steam of his cooking pot unless he gives him a ladle from it. And he does not buy fruit for his children so that they go out with it to his neighbour's children, and they do not feed them from it." Then the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Take heed," and "only a few of you will take heed."

**The second issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So make peace between your two brothers﴾. That is, between any two Muslims who are in dispute. It has also been said: between the Aws and the Khazraj, as has already been mentioned.

Abu Ali said: He intended by "the two brothers" the two groups, because the dual form may be used while the intended meaning is plurality, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Rather, both His hands are outstretched﴾ [Surah al-Ma'idah, 5:64].

Abu Ubaydah said: That is, make peace between every two brothers, so it applies to all of them.

Ibn Sirin, Nasr ibn Asim, Abu al-Aliyah, al-Jahdari and Ya'qub read "bayna ikhwatikum" with the tā' in the plural form. Al-Hasan read "ikhwanikum." The rest read "akhawaykum" with the yā' in the dual form.

**The third issue:** In this verse and the one before it there is evidence that rebellion (baghy) does not remove the name of faith, because Allah, Exalted is He, called them believing brothers although they were rebels.

Al-Harith al-A'war said: Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, who was the exemplar, was asked about fighting the people of rebellion from the people of the Camel and Siffin: "Are they polytheists?" He said: "No, they fled from polytheism." It was asked: "Are they hypocrites?" He said: "No, for the hypocrites do not mention Allah except a little." He was asked: "Then what is their state?" He said: "They are our brothers who have rebelled against us."

**Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 49, verse 11 (part 1 of 2)**

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, let not a people ridicule [another] people, perhaps they may be better than them; nor let women ridicule [other] women, perhaps they may be better than them.﴾ In this there are four issues.

The first issue: "O you who have believed, let not a people ridicule [another] people, perhaps they may be better than them." It was said: better in the sight of Allah. It was also said: "better than them" means better in belief, and sounder inwardly. Al-sukhriyah (ridicule) is mockery (al-istihza'). One says: sakhirtu minhu, asjaru sakharan (with a fathah on the kha'), wa-masKHaran and sukhran (with a dammah). Abu Zayd related: sakhirtu bihi, and it is the weaker of the two dialects. Al-Akhfash said: sakhirtu minhu and sakhirtu bihi, and dahiktu minhu and dahiktu bihi, and hazi'tu minhu and hazi'tu bihi; all are said. The noun is al-sukhriyah and al-sukhri, and both were recited for His saying: ﴿so that some of them may take others as subservient [sukhriyyan]﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 32], which has already been discussed [[Verse 32 of Surah al-Zukhruf; see p. 83 of this part, and vol. 12 p. 154 and vol. 15 p. 225]]. And "fulanun sukhrah" means one who is made to work as a servant; one says "khadimu sukhrah" (a forced-labour servant). "Rajulu sukhrah" also means a man who is mocked. And "sukhara" (with a fathah on the kha') means one who mocks people.

The second issue: The occasion of its revelation has been disputed. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was revealed concerning Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, who was hard of hearing. Whenever he came, people would make room for him so that he could sit beside the Prophet (ﷺ) and hear what he said. One day he came after having missed a rak'ah of the dawn prayer with the Prophet (ﷺ). When the Prophet (ﷺ) finished, his companions took their seats, and each man settled into his place and clung to it, so that no one would make room for anyone, until a man could find no place and remained standing. When Thabit finished the prayer, he stepped over people's necks saying, "Make room, make room!" They made room for him until he reached the Prophet (ﷺ), with a man between him and the Prophet (ﷺ). He said to the man, "Make room!" The man replied, "You have found a seat, so sit down!" Thabit sat behind him in anger, then said, "Who is this?" They said, "So-and-so." Thabit said, "The son of so-and-so!" reproaching him with a mother he had had in the Jahiliyyah. The man was ashamed, and so it was revealed.

Al-Dahhak said: it was revealed concerning the delegation of Banu Tamim whose mention was made at the beginning of the "surah" [[See pp. 300 and 304]]. They mocked the poor among the Companions, such as 'Ammar, Khabbab, Ibn Fuhayrah, Bilal, Suhayb, Salman, Salim the freed slave of Abu Hudhayfah, and others, because of the shabbiness of their condition; so it was revealed concerning those of them who had believed.

Mujahid said: it is the mockery of the rich toward the poor.

Ibn Zayd said: let not one whom Allah has covered his sins mock one whom Allah has exposed, for perhaps the exposure of his sins in this world is better for him in the Hereafter.

It was also said: it was revealed concerning 'Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl when he came to Madinah as a Muslim. Whenever the Muslims saw him, they would say, "The son of Pharaoh of this community!" He complained of this to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and so it was revealed.

In sum, no one should dare to mock someone whom he sees with his own eyes in shabby condition, or with a physical affliction, or who is not adept (laybiq) in conversation [[A man is called laybiq or labiq: skilled and gentle in every work]]. For perhaps that person is more sincere in his inner self and purer of heart than one who is the opposite of his description; he then wrongs himself by belittling one whom Allah has honoured and by mocking one whom Allah has exalted. The righteous predecessors (al-salaf) went to such an extreme in guarding and restraining themselves from this that 'Amr ibn Shurahbil said: "If I saw a man suckling a she-goat and laughed at him, I would fear that I would do the same thing." And from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud: "Affliction is entrusted to speech. Even if I mocked a dog, I would fear that I might be turned into a dog."

In the language, "qawm" is specifically for males. Zuhayr said:

*"I do not know, and I will think I know: are the family of Hisn a 'qawm' or 'nisa'?"*

They were called qawm because they stand (yaqumuna) with their caller in hardships. It was also said that it is the plural of qa'im (standing), and then it was used for every group even if they are not standing. Women may enter the qawm figuratively, and this has been explained previously in al-Baqarah.

The third issue: His saying: ﴿nor let women ridicule [other] women, perhaps they may be better than them.﴾ He singled out women for mention because mockery of them is more frequent. Allah has said: ﴿Indeed, We sent Noah to his people﴾ [Nuh: 1], which includes all of them. The exegetes said: it was revealed concerning two of the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) who mocked Umm Salamah. This was because she tied her waist with a sibiyyah, which is a white garment (and similar to it is al-sibb), and let its two ends hang behind her, so that she would drag it. 'A'ishah said to Hafsah, may Allah be pleased with them both: "Look! What she drags behind her is like the tongue of a dog!" This was their mockery. Anas and Ibn Zayd said: it was revealed concerning the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), who reproached Umm Salamah for her shortness. It was also said: it was revealed concerning 'A'ishah, who gestured with her hand toward Umm Salamah and said, "O Prophet of Allah, she is truly short!"

'Ikrimah related from Ibn 'Abbas: Safiyyah bint Huyayy ibn Akhtab came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said, "O Messenger of Allah, the women reproach me and say to me, 'O Jewess, daughter of two Jews!'" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: [Why did you not say: "My father is Harun, my paternal uncle is Musa, and my husband is Muhammad"?] So Allah revealed this verse.

The fourth issue: In the Sahih of al-Tirmidhi, from 'A'ishah, she said: "I imitated a man for the Prophet (ﷺ)," and he said: [I would not like to have imitated a man, even if I were given such-and-such.] She said: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, Safiyyah is a woman,'" and she gestured with her hand, meaning that she is short. He said: [You have said a word which, if it were mixed with the sea, would have mixed it.] [[The Arabs use "qawl" as an expression for all actions, and apply it to other than speech and the tongue, figuratively and by extension]]

In al-Bukhari, from 'Abdullah ibn Zam'ah, he said: The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade a man to laugh at what comes out of the bodies [of others]. And he said: [Why does one of you beat his wife like a stallion beats a mare, then perhaps embrace her?]

In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: [Indeed Allah does not look at your forms or your wealth, but He looks at your hearts and your deeds.]

This is a great hadith, and it entails that one should not pass definitive judgment on anyone's fault because of the appearance of acts of obedience or disobedience on him. For perhaps one who guards the outward deeds is one in whose heart Allah knows a blameworthy quality that invalidates those deeds; and perhaps one whom we see as negligent or disobedient is one in whose heart Allah knows a praiseworthy quality by which He forgives him. Thus deeds are probable indicators, not decisive proofs. And it entails that we should not exaggerate in exalting one whom we see doing righteous deeds, nor hold in contempt a Muslim whom we see doing evil deeds. Rather, that evil state is to be despised and condemned, not the blameworthy person himself. So reflect on this, for it is a subtle insight, and success is from Allah.

His saying: ﴿and do not defame one another﴾ has three issues. His saying: ﴿and do not defame one another﴾. Al-lamz is faultfinding (al-ayb). It has passed in Bara'ah at His saying: ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the charities﴾ [[vol. 8 p. 166]] [al-Tawbah: 58]. Al-Tabari said: al-lamz is by the hand, the eye, the tongue, and gesture; while al-hamz is only by the tongue. This verse is like His saying: ﴿and do not kill yourselves﴾ [[verse 29 of Surah al-Nisa']] [al-Nisa': 29], meaning that none of you should kill another, because the believers are like a single soul, so that by killing his brother he has in effect killed himself. And like His saying: ﴿then greet one another﴾ [[verse 61 of Surah al-Nur]] [al-Nur: 61], meaning that some of you should greet others. The meaning is: let none of you find fault with another. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: let none of you slander another. Al-Dahhak said: let none of you curse another. And it was recited as "wa-la talmuzu" with a dammah.

In His saying "anfusakum" there is an admonition that a sensible person does not find fault with himself, and so he should not find fault with another, since the other is like himself. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: [The believers are like one body; if one limb complains, the whole body responds to it with sleeplessness and fever.]

Bakr ibn 'Abdullah al-Muzani said: If you want to see many faults, then consider the faultfinder, for he only faults people for the excess of faults in himself.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: [One of you sees the speck [[al-qadhah: anything that falls into the eye, water, or dust, such as dirt, chaff, filth, or the like]] in his brother's eye, and leaves the trunk in his own eye.]

It was also said: part of a man's happiness is that he occupies himself with the faults of his own self rather than the faults of others. A poet said:

*"The man, if he is wise and scrupulous, his scrupulousness occupies him from his faults,*
*Just as the sick, ailing person is occupied by his own ailment from the ailments of all people."*

Another said:

*"Do not expose the faults of people that they have concealed, lest Allah expose a veil over your own faults.*
*And mention the good qualities of them when they are mentioned, and do not reproach any of them for what is in you."*

The second matter: His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And do not insult one another with nicknames﴾. *Al-nabaz* (with a vowel on the *ba*) means a nickname, and its plural is *al-anbaz*. *Al-nabz* (with the *ba* unvowelled) is the verbal noun. You say, "He *nabazahu* (insults him with a nickname), *yanbizuhu*, *nabzan*," meaning he gave him a nickname. "So-and-so *yunabbiz* the children," meaning he gives them nicknames, with the doubled letter for frequency. It is also said that *al-nabaz* and *al-nazab* mean a bad nickname. *Tanabazu bil-alqab* means that some of them gave nicknames to others.

In al-Tirmidhi, from Abu Jubayra ibn al-Dahhak, who said: "A man among us would have two or three names, and he would be called by some of them, so he might dislike that. Then this verse was revealed: ﴿And do not insult one another with nicknames﴾." He said: "This is a good (*hasan*) hadith." This Abu Jubayra is the brother of Thabit ibn al-Dahhak ibn Khalifa al-Ansari. Abu Zayd [[Abu Zayd is one of the narrators in the chain of this hadith.]] Sa'id ibn al-Rabi', the companion of al-Harawi, is trustworthy (*thiqa*).

In the Musannaf of Abu Dawud, from him (i.e., Abu Zayd), he said: "This verse was revealed concerning us, the Banu Salama: ﴿And do not insult one another with nicknames; how evil is the name of wickedness after faith﴾." He said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ came, and there was not a man among us who did not have two or three names. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ would say, 'O so-and-so,' and they would say, 'Wait, O Messenger of Allah, he becomes angry at this name.' Then this verse was revealed: ﴿And do not insult one another with nicknames﴾."

This is one opinion. The second opinion: al-Hasan and Mujahid said: a man would be reproached after his conversion for his former disbelief, saying, "O Jew! O Christian!" So this verse was revealed. This was also narrated from Qatada, Abu al-'Aliya and 'Ikrima. Qatada said: it is the saying of a man to another man, "O sinner! O hypocrite!" Mujahid and al-Hasan also said this.

﴿How evil is the name of wickedness after faith﴾: that is, how evil it is for a man to be named a disbeliever or an adulterer after his Islam and repentance. This was said by Ibn Zayd. It has also been said: the meaning is that whoever gives a nickname to his brother or mocks him, he is a sinner (*fasiq*). In the Sahih: "Whoever says to his brother, 'O disbeliever!', one of them has indeed deserved it: if it is as he said, well; otherwise it returns upon him." So whoever does what Allah has forbidden of mockery, mocking and nicknaming, that is wickedness (*fusuq*), and that is not permitted.

It is narrated that Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, was with the Prophet ﷺ when a man quarrelled with him, and Abu Dharr said to him, "O son of the Jewish woman!" The Prophet ﷺ said: "You see no superiority here of a red man or a black man over you, except in piety." And this verse was revealed: ﴿And do not insult one another with nicknames﴾.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "Insulting one another with nicknames" means that a man has committed bad deeds and then repented, and Allah forbade that he be reproached for what has passed. This is supported by what is narrated: the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever reproaches a believer for a sin from which he has repented, it is binding upon Allah to test him with it and expose him in it, in this world and the Hereafter."

The third matter: there is an exception from this, which is the one whose name has become dominant through use, like al-A'raj (the lame) and al-Ahdab (the hunchbacked), when he has no choice in it and does not feel offended by it. The community has permitted this, and the people of the religion (*ahl al-milla*) agree on its use. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "By Allah's life, there has come into their books of this kind what I do not approve in a righteous man, such as Jazra, Salih ibn Muhammad ibn 'Amr ibn Habib, Abu 'Ali al-Baghdadi, the hafiz. Al-Khatib al-Baghdadi related with his chain… I heard Salih (i.e., Jazra) say: 'Some shaykhs came to us from Syria, and I read to him: Jarir ibn 'Uthman related to us, he said: Abu Umama had a bead (*khurza*) with which he would treat the sick, and I mispronounced 'khurza' as 'jazra' and said: 'Abu Umama had a jazra,' whereas it is khurza.'" See the Tarikh Baghdad, vol. 9, p. 322, in the biography of this Salih.

He was called Jazra because he mispronounced "khurza." Likewise their saying about Muhammad ibn Sulayman al-Hadrami: Muttayyan, because he fell into mud (*tin*). Things like that have become dominant among later people, and I do not think it is lawful in religion." Musa ibn 'Ali ibn Rabah al-Misri used to say: "I do not make lawful anyone who diminutivised my father's name," and the dominant form of his name was the diminutive with a *damma* on the *'ayn*.

What governs all of this is that anything a person dislikes being called is not permitted when used to hurt him. And Allah knows best.

I say: On this meaning al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, gave a chapter heading in the Book of Good Manners (*Kitab al-Adab*) of his Sahih Jami': "Chapter: What is permitted of mentioning people, such as their saying 'the tall one' and 'the short one,' when it is not meant to shame the man." He said: "The Prophet ﷺ said: 'What does Dhu al-Yadayn say?'" Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: The verse includes the prohibition of nicknaming a person with what he dislikes, and it is permitted to nickname him with what he loves. Do you not see that the Prophet ﷺ gave 'Umar the title al-Faruq, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, 'Uthman Dhu al-Nurayn, Khuzayma Dhu al-Shahadatayn, and Abu Hurayra Dhu al-Shimalayn and Dhu al-Yadayn, and similar cases.

Al-Zamakhshari: "It is related from the Prophet ﷺ: 'It is among the rights of a believer over a believer that he calls him by his most beloved of names to him.'" For this reason, the kunya (teknonym, a name formed with "Abu" or "Umm") is part of the Sunnah and good manners. 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Spread the kunyas, for they are a reminder." Abu Bakr was given the titles al-'Atiq and al-Siddiq, 'Umar al-Faruq, Hamza Asad Allah (the Lion of Allah), and Khalid Sayf Allah (the Sword of Allah). Few of the famous figures in the Jahiliyya and Islam have been without a title. These good titles have continued among all nations, Arab and non-Arab, in their speech and correspondence without objection."

Al-Mawardi said: As for those titles that are desirable and praiseworthy, they are not disliked. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ described a number of his companions with qualities that became for them among the noblest of titles.

I say: As for those whose apparent meaning is disliked, when they are intended as a description and not as an insult, that is very common.
